prompt: **Problem 2.0.1.** A *$\sigma$-algebra* on a set $X$ is a family $\Sigma$ of subsets of $X$ containing $\varnothing$, closed under complements and under countable unions and countable intersections. A *measure* on $(X,\Sigma)$ is a function $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ and $\mu(\bigcup E_i)=\sum\mu(E_i)$ for pairwise disjoint $E_1,E_2,\ldots\in\Sigma$. Which of the following are $\sigma$-algebras over $X=\{0,1,2,3,4\}$? (1) $\{\varnothing,X\}$; (2) $\{\varnothing,\{0\},\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{4\},X\}$; (3) $\{\varnothing,\{0,1\},\{2,3,4\},X\}$; (4) $\{\varnothing,\{0\},\{1\},\{0,1\},\{1,2\},\{1,2,3,4\},\{0,2,3,4\},X\}$. Answer with the numbers of those that are, e.g. "1 and 2".

solutions.title: Test closure
solutions.body:
(1) Yes: complement of $\varnothing$ is $X$ and vice versa; unions and intersections stay in the family.

(2) No: $\{0\}\in\Sigma$ but its complement $\{1,2,3,4\}\notin\Sigma$.

(3) Yes: $\{0,1\}$ and $\{2,3,4\}$ are complements of each other, and any union/intersection of members is a member.

(4) No: $\{0,1\}\in\Sigma$ but its complement $\{2,3,4\}\notin\Sigma$ (also $\{0\}\cup\{1,2\}=\{0,1,2\}\notin\Sigma$).

**Answer: 1 and 3**

prompt: **Problem 2.0.5.** A *$\sigma$-algebra* on a set $X$ is a family $\Sigma$ of subsets of $X$ containing $\varnothing$, closed under complements and under countable unions and countable intersections. A *measure* on $(X,\Sigma)$ is a function $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ and $\mu(\bigcup E_i)=\sum\mu(E_i)$ for pairwise disjoint $E_1,E_2,\ldots\in\Sigma$. Let $X$ be any set, $\Sigma=\mathcal P(X)$ (all subsets), and fix $x_0\in X$. Define $\mu(A)=1$ if $x_0\in A$ and $\mu(A)=0$ otherwise. Is $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ a measure space? (Yes/No)

solutions.title: Check the axioms
solutions.body:
$\mathcal P(X)$ is a $\sigma$-algebra. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ and $\mu\ge0$. For pairwise disjoint $E_i$, at most one of them contains $x_0$. If one does, then $\bigcup E_i\ni x_0$ and $\mu(\bigcup E_i)=1=\sum\mu(E_i)$; if none does, both sides are $0$. So $\mu$ is a measure (the *Dirac measure*).

**Answer: Yes**

prompt: **Problem 2.1.2.** For $S\subset\mathbb R^n$ let $|S|=\sup_{x,y\in S}|x-y|$ be its diameter. For $\delta>0$ a *$\delta$-cover* of $F\subset\mathbb R^n$ is a finite or countable family $\{U_i\}$ with $F\subset\bigcup U_i$ and $|U_i|<\delta$. Put $H^s_\delta(F)=\inf\{\sum_i|U_i|^s:\{U_i\}\text{ a }\delta\text{-cover of }F\}$ and $H^s(F)=\lim_{\delta\to0}H^s_\delta(F)$ (the $s$-dimensional Hausdorff measure). Which of the following are $\delta$-covers of $[0,1]\subset\mathbb R$ for $\delta=\frac12$? (1) $\{(-\frac13,\frac13),(\frac13,\frac23),(\frac23,\frac43)\}$; (2) $\{[0,\frac1n]:n\in\mathbb N\}$; (3) $\{[0,\frac12],[\frac12,1]\}$. Answer with the numbers, or "none".

solutions.title: Check both conditions
solutions.body:
A $\delta$-cover needs (i) the sets cover $[0,1]$ and (ii) every set has diameter strictly less than $\frac12$.

(1) $|(-\frac13,\frac13)|=\frac23>\frac12$ (and the point $\frac13$ is not covered). Fails.

(2) The set $[0,\frac11]=[0,1]$ (for $n=1$) has diameter $1\ge\frac12$, and so do $[0,\frac12]$ ($n=2$, diameter exactly $\frac12$). Fails.

(3) Both sets have diameter exactly $\frac12$, not $<\frac12$. Fails.

**Answer: none**

prompt: **Problem 2.0.4 (Countable subadditivity).** A *$\sigma$-algebra* on a set $X$ is a family $\Sigma$ of subsets of $X$ containing $\varnothing$, closed under complements and under countable unions and countable intersections. A *measure* on $(X,\Sigma)$ is a function $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ and $\mu(\bigcup E_i)=\sum\mu(E_i)$ for pairwise disjoint $E_1,E_2,\ldots\in\Sigma$. Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space. Show that for any countable collection $E_1,E_2,\ldots\in\Sigma$, $$\mu\Big(\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty E_i\Big)\le\sum_{i=1}^\infty\mu(E_i).$$ (You may use monotonicity: $A\subset B\Rightarrow\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.)

solutions.title: Disjointification
solutions.body:
Let $F_1=E_1$ and $F_i=E_i\setminus(E_1\cup\dots\cup E_{i-1})$. Each $F_i\in\Sigma$ (complements and intersections are allowed), the $F_i$ are pairwise disjoint, $F_i\subset E_i$, and $\bigcup F_i=\bigcup E_i$. By countable additivity and monotonicity,
$$\mu\Big(\bigcup E_i\Big)=\mu\Big(\bigcup F_i\Big)=\sum\mu(F_i)\le\sum\mu(E_i).$$
(Monotonicity itself: if $A\subset B$ then $\mu(B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B\setminus A)\ge\mu(A)$.) $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.1.3.** For $S\subset\mathbb R^n$ let $|S|=\sup_{x,y\in S}|x-y|$ be its diameter. For $\delta>0$ a *$\delta$-cover* of $F\subset\mathbb R^n$ is a finite or countable family $\{U_i\}$ with $F\subset\bigcup U_i$ and $|U_i|<\delta$. Put $H^s_\delta(F)=\inf\{\sum_i|U_i|^s:\{U_i\}\text{ a }\delta\text{-cover of }F\}$ and $H^s(F)=\lim_{\delta\to0}H^s_\delta(F)$ (the $s$-dimensional Hausdorff measure). Let $0<\delta_1<\delta_2$. Show that $H^s_{\delta_1}(F)\ge H^s_{\delta_2}(F)$, and conclude that $\lim_{\delta\to0}H^s_\delta(F)$ exists in $[0,\infty]$.
answer: Every $\delta_1$-cover is a $\delta_2$-cover, so the infimum over fewer covers is larger.

solutions.title: Compare the sets of covers
solutions.body:
A $\delta_1$-cover has all $|U_i|<\delta_1<\delta_2$, so it is also a $\delta_2$-cover. Thus the infimum defining $H^s_{\delta_2}$ is taken over a larger family of covers and is at most the infimum defining $H^s_{\delta_1}$.

Hence $\delta\mapsto H^s_\delta(F)$ is non-increasing as $\delta$ increases, i.e. non-decreasing as $\delta\downarrow0$, so the limit as $\delta\to0$ exists (possibly $\infty$) as a supremum. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.1.9.** For $S\subset\mathbb R^n$ let $|S|=\sup_{x,y\in S}|x-y|$ be its diameter. For $\delta>0$ a *$\delta$-cover* of $F\subset\mathbb R^n$ is a finite or countable family $\{U_i\}$ with $F\subset\bigcup U_i$ and $|U_i|<\delta$. Put $H^s_\delta(F)=\inf\{\sum_i|U_i|^s:\{U_i\}\text{ a }\delta\text{-cover of }F\}$ and $H^s(F)=\lim_{\delta\to0}H^s_\delta(F)$ (the $s$-dimensional Hausdorff measure). (For $s=0$ use the convention $|U|^0=1$ for every non-empty set $U$.) Prove that $H^0$ is the counting measure: $H^0(F)=\#F$ (and $\infty$ if $F$ is infinite).
answer: For small $\delta$ every set of a $\delta$-cover contains at most as many points as ... one point; so one needs at least $\#F$ sets.

solutions.title: Small $\delta$ separates points
solutions.body:
With the convention, $\sum|U_i|^0$ is the number of (non-empty) sets in the cover.

*$F$ finite with $N$ points.* Let $d$ be the smallest distance between two distinct points of $F$. For $\delta\le d$, a set of diameter $<\delta$ contains at most one point of $F$, so any $\delta$-cover needs at least $N$ sets; the $N$ singletons (diameter $0<\delta$) form a $\delta$-cover. So $H^0_\delta(F)=N$ for all small $\delta$ and $H^0(F)=N$.

*$F$ infinite.* For any $M$ pick $M$ points of $F$ with minimum mutual distance $d_M>0$. For $\delta\le d_M$ every $\delta$-cover of $F$ needs $\ge M$ sets, so $H^0_\delta(F)\ge M$. Since $M$ is arbitrary, $H^0(F)=\infty$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.1.7.** For $S\subset\mathbb R^n$ let $|S|=\sup_{x,y\in S}|x-y|$ be its diameter. For $\delta>0$ a *$\delta$-cover* of $F\subset\mathbb R^n$ is a finite or countable family $\{U_i\}$ with $F\subset\bigcup U_i$ and $|U_i|<\delta$. Put $H^s_\delta(F)=\inf\{\sum_i|U_i|^s:\{U_i\}\text{ a }\delta\text{-cover of }F\}$ and $H^s(F)=\lim_{\delta\to0}H^s_\delta(F)$ (the $s$-dimensional Hausdorff measure). Let $0<r<s$ and $E\subset\mathbb R^n$. Prove: (1) $H^r(E)\ge H^s(E)$; (2) if $H^r(E)<\infty$ then $H^s(E)=0$.

solutions.title: Compare $|U|^s$ with $|U|^r$
solutions.body:
Fix $0<\delta<1$ and a $\delta$-cover $\{U_i\}$ of $E$. Since $|U_i|<\delta<1$ and $s>r$,
$$|U_i|^s=|U_i|^{s-r}|U_i|^r\le\delta^{s-r}|U_i|^r\le|U_i|^r.$$
Summing and taking the infimum over all $\delta$-covers gives
$$H^s_\delta(E)\le\delta^{s-r}H^r_\delta(E)\le H^r_\delta(E).$$
(1) Let $\delta\to0$: $H^s(E)\le H^r(E)$.

(2) If $H^r(E)<\infty$, then $H^r_\delta(E)\le H^r(E)$ for all $\delta$, so $H^s_\delta(E)\le\delta^{s-r}H^r(E)\to0$ as $\delta\to0$ (note $s-r>0$). Hence $H^s(E)=0$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 2.1.8.** For $S\subset\mathbb R^n$ let $|S|=\sup_{x,y\in S}|x-y|$ be its diameter. For $\delta>0$ a *$\delta$-cover* of $F\subset\mathbb R^n$ is a finite or countable family $\{U_i\}$ with $F\subset\bigcup U_i$ and $|U_i|<\delta$. Put $H^s_\delta(F)=\inf\{\sum_i|U_i|^s:\{U_i\}\text{ a }\delta\text{-cover of }F\}$ and $H^s(F)=\lim_{\delta\to0}H^s_\delta(F)$ (the $s$-dimensional Hausdorff measure). (The Hausdorff dimension of $E$ is the critical value $s_0$ with $H^s(E)=\infty$ for $s<s_0$ and $H^s(E)=0$ for $s>s_0$.) Prove that every $E\subset\mathbb R^n$ has Hausdorff dimension at most $n$, i.e. $H^s(E)=0$ for every $s>n$. You may use countable subadditivity of $H^s$.
answer: Cover bounded pieces by $\sim\ell^{-n}$ cubes of side $\ell$; the sum is $\sim\ell^{s-n}\to0$.

solutions.title: Cover by small cubes
solutions.body:
Let $s>n$. Write $E=\bigcup_{k\ge1}E_k$ with $E_k=E\cap[-k,k]^n$; by countable subadditivity it suffices to show $H^s(E_k)=0$ for each $k$.

Fix $k$, $\delta>0$, and choose $\ell>0$ with $\sqrt n\,\ell<\delta$. Cut $[-k,k]^n$ into $N=\lceil2k/\ell\rceil^n\le(2k/\ell+1)^n$ cubes of side $\ell$, each of diameter $\sqrt n\,\ell<\delta$. They form a $\delta$-cover of $E_k$, so
$$H^s_\delta(E_k)\le N(\sqrt n\,\ell)^s\le\Big(\tfrac{2k}\ell+1\Big)^n n^{s/2}\ell^s\le(2k+\ell)^nn^{s/2}\,\ell^{\,s-n}.$$
As $\ell\to0$ this tends to $0$ because $s-n>0$ (this may be done for every $\delta$, taking $\ell\to0$ and then $\delta\to0$). So $H^s(E_k)=0$ and hence $H^s(E)=0$ for all $s>n$; the critical value is at most $n$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.0.1.** A map $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ is a *contraction* if there is $0<c<1$ with $|f(x)-f(y)|=c|x-y|$ for all $x,y$ (with $\le$ the proof of (1) is the same). Write $f^{(k)}$ for the $k$-fold composition. (1) Show that for all $x,y$ and $\epsilon>0$ some $k$ has $|f^{(k)}(x)-f^{(k)}(y)|<\epsilon$. (2) Show that if the contraction hypothesis is weakened to $|f(x)-f(y)|<|x-y|$ for $x\ne y$, there are such maps with no fixed point.

solutions.title: Iterate the bound; build a counterexample
solutions.body:
(1) By induction $|f^{(k)}(x)-f^{(k)}(y)|\le c^k|x-y|$. Since $0<c<1$, $c^k\to0$, so choose $k$ with $c^k|x-y|<\epsilon$.

(2) On $\mathbb R$ let $f(x)=x+\frac1{1+e^x}$. Then $f'(x)=1-\frac{e^x}{(1+e^x)^2}\in[\frac34,1)$, since $\frac{e^x}{(1+e^x)^2}\in(0,\frac14]$. By the mean value theorem, for $x\ne y$, $|f(x)-f(y)|=f'(\xi)|x-y|<|x-y|$. But $f(x)=x$ would require $\frac1{1+e^x}=0$, which never happens. So $f$ has no fixed point (it is not a contraction with a uniform constant $c<1$, since $f'(x)\to1$ as $x\to-\infty$). $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.1.1.** Let $f_1,f_2,f_3:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$, $f_1(x)=\frac12x$, $f_2(x)=\frac12x+(\frac12,0)$, $f_3(x)=\frac12x+(\frac14,\frac{\sqrt3}4)$. Its attractor is the Sierpinski triangle. An IFS satisfies the *open set condition* (OSC) if there is a bounded non-empty open $U$ with $f_i(U)\cap f_j(U)=\varnothing$ ($i\neq j$) and $f_i(U)\subset U$. If an IFS with contraction ratios $c_i$ satisfies the OSC, the Hausdorff dimension of its attractor is the unique $s$ with $\sum c_i^s=1$. Show that this IFS satisfies the OSC and compute the Hausdorff dimension of its attractor.

solutions.title: Open triangle and $3\cdot2^{-s}=1$
solutions.body:
Let $U$ be the open equilateral triangle with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2)$. Each $f_i$ halves it and moves it to one corner: $f_1(U),f_2(U),f_3(U)$ are the three open corner triangles of side $\frac12$. They are pairwise disjoint (the open middle triangle and the common vertices/edges are excluded) and each lies in $U$. So the OSC holds.

All ratios are $\frac12$, so we need $3\left(\frac12\right)^s=1$, i.e. $2^s=3$, $s=\frac{\ln3}{\ln2}\approx1.585$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{\ln3}{\ln2}$**

prompt: **Problem 4.1.2 (Koch curve).** The Koch curve $K$ is built from $K_0=[0,1]$: at each stage every segment is replaced by $4$ segments of one third its length (as in the usual Koch construction), so $K$ is the attractor of an IFS of $4$ similarities each with contraction ratio $\frac13$, and this IFS satisfies the open set condition. For such an IFS the Hausdorff dimension of the attractor is the unique $s$ with $\sum c_i^s=1$. Find the Hausdorff dimension of $K$.

solutions.title: Solve $4\cdot3^{-s}=1$
solutions.body:
With four maps of ratio $\frac13$: $4\left(\frac13\right)^s=1\iff3^s=4\iff s=\frac{\ln4}{\ln3}\approx1.2619$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{\ln4}{\ln3}$**

prompt: **Problem 4.1.3.** The Cantor set $C$ has Hausdorff dimension $s=\frac{\ln2}{\ln3}>0$ and $H^s(C)\ge\frac12>0$ (mass distribution principle). Use this to prove that $C$ is uncountable.
answer: A countable set has $H^s=0$ for every $s>0$.

solutions.title: Countable sets are null
solutions.body: A single point $\{p\}$ has $H^s(\{p\})=0$ for $s>0$: it is covered by the single set $\{p\}$ of diameter $0<\delta$, giving $H^s_\delta(\{p\})=0$ for every $\delta$. If $C$ were countable, $C=\{p_1,p_2,\dots\}$, countable subadditivity would give $H^s(C)\le\sum H^s(\{p_i\})=0$, contradicting $H^s(C)\ge\frac12$. Hence $C$ is uncountable. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.2.1.** For $S\subset\mathbb R^n$ let $|S|=\sup_{x,y\in S}|x-y|$ be its diameter. For $\delta>0$ a *$\delta$-cover* of $F\subset\mathbb R^n$ is a finite or countable family $\{U_i\}$ with $F\subset\bigcup U_i$ and $|U_i|<\delta$. Put $H^s_\delta(F)=\inf\{\sum_i|U_i|^s:\{U_i\}\text{ a }\delta\text{-cover of }F\}$ and $H^s(F)=\lim_{\delta\to0}H^s_\delta(F)$ (the $s$-dimensional Hausdorff measure). Using the *mass distribution principle* (if $\mu$ is a measure on $F$ with $0<\mu(F)<\infty$ and $\mu(U)\le c|U|^s$ for all $U\subset F$ with $|U|\le\epsilon$, then $H^s(F)\ge\mu(F)/c$), and the fact that $H^r(E)<\infty\Rightarrow H^s(E)=0$ for $s>r$, prove that the real line has Hausdorff dimension $1$ but $H^1(\mathbb R)=\infty$.
answer: Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$ gives $H^1\ge1$; $N$ intervals of length $1/N$ give $H^s=0$ for $s>1$; $[0,k]\subset\mathbb R$ gives $H^1\ge k$.

solutions.title: Work on $[0,1]$ first
solutions.body:
Let $\lambda$ be Lebesgue measure on $F=[0,1]$. A set $U\subset F$ lies in an interval of length $|U|$, so $\lambda(U)\le|U|$. The mass distribution principle (with $c=1$, $s=1$) gives $H^1([0,1])\ge1>0$.

*Dimension $\ge1$:* if $H^s([0,1])<\infty$ for some $s<1$ then $H^1([0,1])=0$, a contradiction. So $H^s([0,1])=\infty$ for $s<1$.

*Dimension $\le1$:* for $s>1$ and $N>1/\delta$, cover $[0,1]$ by $N$ intervals of length $\frac1N<\delta$: $H^s_\delta\le N\cdot N^{-s}=N^{1-s}\to0$. So $H^s([0,1])=0$ for $s>1$.

Hence $\dim[0,1]=1$. For $\mathbb R$: it contains $[0,k]$, a scaled copy of $[0,1]$, so by homogeneity ($H^1(cE)=cH^1(E)$) and monotonicity, $H^1(\mathbb R)\ge H^1([0,k])=kH^1([0,1])\ge k$ for every $k$; so $H^1(\mathbb R)=\infty$. Also $H^s(\mathbb R)\ge H^s([0,1])=\infty$ for $s<1$, and for $s>1$, $H^s(\mathbb R)\le\sum_kH^s([-k,k])=0$ by subadditivity. So the dimension of $\mathbb R$ is $1$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 4.2.3.** Give an explicit lower bound $>0$ on the Hausdorff measure of the Cantor dust $C\times C\subset\mathbb R^2$ in its dimension $s=\frac{\ln4}{\ln3}$. (Use the mass distribution principle: if $\mu(U)\le c|U|^s$ for small $U$, then $H^s\ge\mu(F)/c$.)
answer: $H^s(C\times C)\ge\frac14$ (using the product of the Cantor measure with itself).

solutions.title: Product Cantor measure
solutions.body:
$C\times C$ is the attractor of four maps of ratio $\frac13$ satisfying the OSC, so its dimension is $s$ with $4\cdot3^{-s}=1$, i.e. $s=\frac{\ln4}{\ln3}$.

Let $\nu$ be the Cantor measure on $C$ giving mass $2^{-k}$ to each level-$k$ interval, and $\mu=\nu\times\nu$, so $\mu(C\times C)=1$ and each level-$k$ square (side $3^{-k}$) has mass $4^{-k}$.

Let $U\subset C\times C$ with $|U|<1$ and choose $k\ge0$ with $3^{-(k+1)}\le|U|<3^{-k}$. Distinct level-$k$ intervals of $C$ are at distance at least $3^{-k}$ apart, so the projections of $U$ (of diameter $<3^{-k}$) each lie in a single level-$k$ interval. Thus $U$ lies in one level-$k$ square and
$$\mu(U)\le4^{-k}=(3^{-k})^s\le(3|U|)^s=3^s|U|^s=4|U|^s,$$
because $3^s=4$. By the mass distribution principle, $H^s(C\times C)\ge\frac{1}{4}$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: **Problem 5.0.2.** Let $S$ be the Sierpinski triangle (attractor of $f_1,f_2,f_3$ above, with $s=\frac{\ln3}{\ln2}$ and natural measure $\mu$ giving mass $3^{-n}$ to each of the $3^n$ scaled copies of side $2^{-n}$). Let $T_n$ be this collection of copies, and $$a_n=\min_{\varnothing\ne\{\Delta_i\}\subset T_n}\frac{\big|\bigcup\Delta_i\big|^s}{\mu\big(\bigcup\Delta_i\big)}.$$ Find $a_1$ and $a_2$.

solutions.title: Compare subsets
solutions.body:
**$n=1$.** The three pieces have side $\frac12$ and mass $\frac13$. One piece: diameter $\frac12$, ratio $\frac{(1/2)^s}{1/3}=\frac{1/3}{1/3}=1$ (as $2^{-s}=\frac13$). Two pieces: their union contains two corners of the big triangle, diameter $1$, mass $\frac23$: ratio $\frac32$. All three: diameter $1$, mass $1$: ratio $1$. So $a_1=1$.

**$n=2$.** There are $9$ pieces of side $\frac14$, each of mass $\frac19$. The extremal choice is the six pieces forming the "ring" around the three corner pieces of the figure, i.e. all pieces except the three at the corners of $S$; their union has diameter $\frac34$ (distance between corresponding vertices of the hexagon-like ring), mass $\frac69=\frac23$, so the ratio is $\left(\frac34\right)^s\cdot\frac32=\frac32\left(\frac34\right)^{\log_23}\approx0.9508$. Checking all $2^9-1$ subsets (the diameter of a union of pieces is the largest distance between corner vertices of the selected triangles; single pieces and the full set give ratio $1$, smaller subsets give larger values) shows nothing beats this, so $a_2\approx0.9508<a_1$.

prompt: **Problem 5.0.3.** With $a_n$ as in Problem 5.0.2 (the minimum of $|\bigcup\Delta_i|^s/\mu(\bigcup\Delta_i)$ over non-empty subfamilies of the $3^n$ pieces of the Sierpinski triangle of side $2^{-n}$), show that $a_{n+1}\le a_n$ for all $n$.
answer: Replace each level-$n$ piece of an optimal family by its three level-$(n+1)$ sub-pieces.

solutions.title: Subdivide
solutions.body: Take a non-empty family of level-$n$ pieces achieving $a_n$, with union $W$. Each level-$n$ piece is the union of three level-$(n+1)$ pieces, so $W$ is also the union of a non-empty family of level-$(n+1)$ pieces. The set $W$ is unchanged, hence so are $|W|$ and $\mu(W)$, and the ratio $|W|^s/\mu(W)$ equals $a_n$. Since $a_{n+1}$ is the minimum over all such families at level $n+1$, $a_{n+1}\le a_n$. $\blacksquare$
